Two parts of `tests/test-claude-sync.sh` failed on 2026-11-25 on the personal MacBook while other suites ran beside them, and passed alone on the same code. One sample each, seen by the builder of #3563.

1. First half, the section "a number handed out is reserved for a few minutes (claude-config#1148)": 4 checks failed in one full run (five sessions asking at once are each given a number; no two the same; the next five with no gap; five asks racing to take over a dead holder's lock). That run read 1884 passed and 4 failed in 591 seconds, with two small suites running beside it. The section alone passed 68 of 68.
2. Second half: one check failed on a time bound (1994 passed, 1 failed), and its section alone passed 71 of 71.

So a busy Mac or a slow CI runner can turn this suite red with no fault in the code. #3680 is about the same suite's length (453 seconds against a 600 second line), which is separate work.

## What done looks like

Each failure reproduced under `tools/load-window.sh` first, with the failing check named. Then each check made to turn on what the code did, never on how long the Mac took: wait on the condition, or set the clock, and where the Mac really cannot be measured, report the part as unmeasured in the shape the runner reads. No time bound is raised to make it pass.

## Open questions

- Are the four reservation checks one fault (the racing sessions sharing a fixed wait) or four?
- Which time bound failed in the second half? The run's output names it; it was not kept in the report.
title: Stop two sections of the claude-sync suite failing when other suites run beside them

body:
The skill helper exits check (`skill-audit.py`, run by `payload/hooks/test-skill-helper-exits.sh`) judges one function at a time. A process started with `subprocess.Popen` and assigned straight to an attribute (`self.x = Popen(...)`) is always a finding, whatever another method reads later. One bound to a local name passes on any single `poll()` or `wait()` in the same function. So the check cannot tell whether a long running process's status is read when it ends.

Seen on 2026-11-25 while fixing pull request 3593: the check rightly failed the monitor's heartbeat process, whose ending was never read. After the fix the check passes because of a `poll()` made right after the first test connection, at the start. The read at the end, which is the real fix, is something the check cannot see; only the unit tests prove it. A change that kept the start check and dropped the read at the end would pass.

## What done looks like

Fixtures first: a long lived process whose ending is read in another method (should pass), one checked only at its start (should fail), and the two shapes above. Then the check follows a process held on an attribute across the methods of its class, or says in its output that it judged only the start. Every finding it gives today on the skills in the repository stays.

## Open questions

- How far should it follow: one class, one file, or helpers the process is handed to?
- Would a count of today's passes that rest on a start check alone show other monitors with the same gap?
title: Make the skill helper exits check see a long lived process whose ending is never read

The check later reminder stops a turn when a memory edit only carries along a future date that was already in the file. `memory_signal` in `payload/hooks/lib/check-later-signals.py:280` scans the whole `new_string` of an Edit for dates ahead of today (line 287) and never compares it with `old_string`, so replacing part of a line that already holds a date reads as a new check left waiting. Seen on 2026-11-25: an edit added a clause to a MEMORY.md index line that had held 2027-09-15 since September, and the turn ended with "This turn left a memory note (MEMORY.md) naming Wed Sep 15". Count only dates that appear in the new text and not in the old text, with a test for an edit whose old and new text share one future date.

## Open questions

Should a Write that replaces a whole memory file also be compared with the file's earlier content? The hook sees only the new content, so it would need the earlier version from the transcript or from disk.
title: Stop the check later reminder firing on a date already in an edited memory line

body:
The rtk hook (`payload/hooks/rtk-rewrite.sh`) still rewrites `grep` into `rtk grep` when something stands in front of it, although each pull writes grep into rtk's excluded list. Seen on 2026-11-25 on the personal MacBook with rtk 0.31.0, one sample each: `FOO=1 grep -h ...` becomes `FOO=1 rtk grep -h ...`, `env grep -h ...` becomes `env rtk grep -h ...`, and `sudo grep -h ...` becomes `sudo rtk grep -h ...`.

`rtk grep -h` prints rtk's help screen and exits 0, so the matches are lost and the command reports success. The same run found that, without the excluded list, a grep over three named files searched only the first. Found by the builder of #3546 while ruling the hook out as that issue's cause.

## What done looks like

Each of the three prefixed shapes reproduced as a failing test of the hook, then the hook refusing any rewrite that lands on `rtk grep` (as it already does for `rtk read`), so a prefixed grep runs as plain grep. The other excluded commands (rg, egrep, fgrep, cat, head, tail) are tried with the same three prefixes, several samples each, and covered the same way where they are rewritten.

## Open questions

- Which other prefixes get past the excluded list (`time`, `nice`, `command`, a path such as `/usr/bin/grep`)?
- rtk refuses to run when its hook file is edited until its hash is recorded again: what is the exact step on each Mac after this merges?
title: Stop the rtk hook rewriting a prefixed grep into rtk grep, which prints help and exits 0

body:
## What happened

On the personal MacBook on 2026-11-25, free space on the data volume fell from 155.0 GB to 67.2 GB between 9:48 and 10:11 AM ET and then stopped. The cause was Dan's own work, as he confirmed by picker that morning. For the next 33 minutes the level moved by 1.4 GB.

`hooks/check-free-space.sh --report` read exit 4 the whole time, and its wording got worse while nothing was being written:

| Time (ET) | Free | What the check said |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10:19 AM | 67.1 GB | falling at about 46.9 GB per hour, zero in about 2 hours |
| 10:31 AM | 67.1 GB | falling at about 90.7 GB per hour, zero in under an hour |
| 10:45 AM | 65.8 GB | falling at about 91.6 GB per hour, zero in under an hour |

The readings are in the kept file for that warning (49 lines, first reading 9:26 AM ET).

## Why

The rate runs from the oldest reading in the six hour window (`FREE_SPACE_WINDOW_HOURS=6`) to the most free space seen in the last 30 minutes (`FREE_SPACE_PERSIST_MIN=30`). For a drop that happens once and stops, the older end stays at the level before the drop until that reading ages out. So the check goes on projecting the drop as a fall still under way. With these numbers it cannot read anything but 4 until about 3:50 PM ET, six hours after the drop began, however flat the disk is.

The recovery rule does not help, because the space has not come back: nothing was given back, it was simply used once.

This is the shape lesson L695 describes: an alert judged by one aggregate over a fixed trailing window cannot stand down until the window clears.

## What it costs

A session treats exit 4 as "start nothing". On 2026-11-25 that stopped every builder start in an orchestrating session for about 45 minutes, until Dan was asked and said to carry on, and it would have stopped them for about five more hours.

It also tells Dan the disk reaches zero in under an hour when it is not moving, which is the false alarm L36 is about.

## What done looks like

1. A failing test first, replaying the kept readings of 2026-11-25 (the check's own replay settings, `FREE_SPACE_NOW` and `FREE_SPACE_BYTES`): today the 10:45 AM reading gives exit 4.
2. A drop that has stopped stands down on recent readings. One way: when the level has held within the recovery margin for the whole of the last `FREE_SPACE_PERSIST_MIN` minutes, the older end of the rate moves to the start of that flat stretch, so the rate is the recent one.
3. A fall that is still under way is still reported no later than it is today. Each earlier case the script's comments record (2026-09-10 at 19 GB an hour, the bursts of #1754, the spike of #3153) keeps its verdict, shown by replaying it.
4. The floor is untouched: under it, exit 3 at once.
5. The wording says when a fall has stopped, with how much went and when, since that is still worth knowing once.

## Open questions

- [x] 3.32 Pull request 3634 (issue #3608, which you told me to file) makes the free space warning speak less, so it needs your word. Today the warning kept saying zero in under an hour for 38 minutes after your Lightroom work stopped taking space, and would have until about 3:50 PM. With the change it stands down once the last 30 minutes alone would not reach zero within six hours. Replaying all nine kept warnings on the personal MacBook (696 readings): four change, all from falling fast to clear, each after a drop that had stopped; no under the floor warning changes. The cost: a fall that pauses 30 minutes or more and then restarts is reported up to 30 minutes later than today (about 9.5 GB at 19 GB an hour). Not replayed on the work MacBook. Merge it? (answered 2026-11-25 ET: we shohuld pretty much always do the work macbook when needed. I do a lot more work there so it'll usually have more data)
- [x] 3.33 Pull request 3634 (the free space warning stands down once a drop has stopped, issue #3608): both Macs have now reported. The work MacBook keeps no free space warnings at all, so it had nothing to replay; its control passed (13 readings changed, all from falling fast to clear, none any other way). So the evidence is the personal MacBook's: nine kept warnings, 696 readings, four warnings change, all from falling fast to clear after a drop that had stopped, and no under the floor warning changes. The cost is unchanged: a fall that pauses 30 minutes or more and then restarts is reported up to 30 minutes later. Merge it? (answered 2026-11-25 ET: 3.33.1 Merge it (Recommended))

1. How long must the level hold flat before the check stands down: the 30 minutes it already uses for a fall that lasts, or longer?
2. Should a stopped drop of this size still be reported once (exit 0 with a line saying 88 GB went between two times), so it is not silent?
3. Does the session rule "exit 3 or 4 means start nothing" need its own wording for a drop Dan says is his?
title: Stand the free space warning down when a single drop has stopped, instead of projecting it for six hours

body:
## Why

"The Claude Tag guide for startups", https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-tag-guide-for-startups, 2026-11-13. The starter instruction in section 01 (triaging alerts) says:

> Check for an existing ticket.

The starter instruction in section 02 (bugs and small features) says:

> Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first.

## What was measured

On 2026-11-24, from `payload/skills/orchestrate/SKILL.md` on origin/main:

- Section 1, Intake (lines 10 to 14), places each item in a repository and checks whether an alert is still firing. It has no step that looks for an issue or pull request that already covers the item.
- The section "Claiming an issue before its builder starts" (from line 36) applies only to "a `build` item whose Source is a GitHub issue". A Slack item that someone already filed, or that another session is already building, is invisible to it.
- `payload/hooks/lib/match-open-issues.py` already matches text against a repository's open issues, for the end of turn review (`payload/hooks/feature-issue-review.sh`, claude-config#256). Nothing else uses it, and it reads issues only, not pull requests.

A print only count over session transcripts on the work MacBook found 62 main sessions that ran /orchestrate, 53 of which read Slack before their first dispatch. 3 of those 53 ran in a folder that is not a git repository and has no issue tracker. Of the 50 in repositories with issues, 4 (8%) read no issue or pull request before dispatching. No case of a Slack item built twice was found: the double build in claude-config#3317 started from a GitHub issue. So this is a low priority guard.

## Change

In the Intake section of `payload/skills/orchestrate/SKILL.md`, for each item that came from Slack and has a repository:

1. Match it against that repository's open issues and open pull requests. Reuse `match-open-issues.py`, extended to read open pull requests as well, or run `gh search issues` and `gh search prs` scoped to the repository.
2. When an issue covers the item, put its number on the board beside the Slack source. For a `build` item, run `claim-issue.sh claim` on that issue before the builder is dispatched, the same as for an item whose source is an issue. The reply in Slack then links the existing issue.
3. A match is shown to the orchestrating session, which reads it and decides. The matcher never rules an item a duplicate by itself, the same stance `match-open-issues.py` takes today.

## What it affects

Today a Slack alert that someone already filed, or a fix already in progress, can be built a second time, and the reply in Slack does not link the issue. The guard closes that gap for one search per Slack item at intake. No harm from the gap has been measured so far, which is why it is low priority.

## Open questions

- [ ] When only an open pull request covers a Slack item, with no issue, what should intake do? (choices: Mark the item covered and do not build / Make it a review of that pull request / Ask Dan each time)
- [ ] Should a match only annotate the board, or hold the item's dispatch until Dan confirms? (choices: Annotate only / Hold until Dan confirms)
title: Check for an existing issue or pull request before orchestrate works a Slack item
